Euro Digital: Europe is preparing money that will work even without the internet

Euro digital has taken a new step forward in Brussels.

The idea is for any citizen to be able to pay with a digital version of the euro, issued by the European Central Bank (ECB), including without an internet connection.

Payments can be made with a phone, card, online, and offline - and rely less on Visa, Mastercard, and private banks.

### What is already raising questions:
- Limits will be set on how much digital euros can be stored.
- Many stores may be required to accept it.
- Banks fear that some of the money will be taken from their accounts.
- Millions of citizens are concerned about privacy of data.

The ECB promises that digital euro will not replace cash, and offline payments will have an increased level of confidentiality (similar to cash).

However, the discussion in Europe has long gone beyond just the technology.

This is a question of power: do we need public digital money or are we opening the door to too much control over how we pay?

📌 The Role of Cryptocurrency in Real Estate Transactions

Main Points
⏺ Cryptocurrencies are becoming a viable alternative for buying, selling, and investing in real estate.
⏺ Blockchain technology offers transparency, security, and faster transactions for property deals.
⏺ This post explores how cryptocurrency is revolutionizing the real estate market.

1️⃣ Faster and Cheaper Transactions: Cryptocurrencies enable faster transactions compared to traditional property deals, which often involve lengthy bank transfers and paperwork.
2️⃣ Decentralized and Secure Payments: Blockchain ensures that real estate transactions are recorded securely and immutably, reducing fraud and errors in property transfers.
3️⃣ Tokenization of Real Estate: Real estate assets can be tokenized, allowing people to own fractional shares in properties, making real estate investment more accessible.
4️⃣ Lower Transaction Fees: Traditional property transactions often involve hefty fees for agents, brokers, and banks. Cryptocurrencies reduce these fees significantly by eliminating intermediaries.
5️⃣ Global Accessibility: Cryptocurrencies enable international buyers to participate in the real estate market without the hassle of currency exchange or complex banking regulations.

Final Thoughts

Cryptocurrency and blockchain are reshaping the real estate market by offering faster, cheaper, and more transparent transactions. As adoption grows, crypto could become the standard for property deals worldwide.

Asylum by GPS: If You’re Not Over the Line, You Don’t Exist

The Supreme Court just turned the border into a legal force field. In a 6–3 ruling, the conservative majority blessed Trump’s power to block asylum seekers on the Mexican side of official crossings and simply refuse to process their claims whenever officials say the line is “too long.” 

As long as a migrant’s toes haven’t crossed the invisible line into U.S. territory, Samuel Alito says they have not “arrived in” the United States at all — so the statutory right to apply for asylum never switches on.

This is the metering policy Obama’s DHS started in 2016, Trump weaponized in 2018, and Biden scrapped in 2021 — now revived in principle by the Court. 

Under metering, CBP officers at ports of entry can cap daily intake and push everyone else back into Mexico, “indefinitely declining” to inspect or register their claims while pretending the law’s promise — that anyone who “arrives in the United States” may seek asylum — only applies once you’re literally over the line. 

The Ninth Circuit had held that approaching a designated crossing counts as arriving and that turning people away violated federal law; the Supreme Court just overruled that, telling border agents they can physically block people at the gate and still call it legal.

Sonia Sotomayor did something she doesn’t do often: she read her dissent from the bench and spelled out what this doctrine means in the real world. 

If you force people to wander along the border hunting for a port that will inspect them, some will die in the desert, some will try to cross illegally and drown or suffocate, and others will give up and be beaten, raped or killed back home for their race, religion, politics or gender. Her line is brutal and obvious: “More people will die.” 

Alito did something just as rare — he fired back from the bench, complaining that he would have given a longer defense if he’d known she planned to air her dissent in court, and insisting that they had merely restated the “ordinary meaning” of arrival.

Trump’s DHS is already treating this as a green light, calling metering an “important tool” to “secure our southern border.” 

The Department’s general counsel actually bragged that they had to go “all the way to SCOTUS” to vindicate the “principle” that someone isn’t in the United States until they physically are — like that was ever in doubt, rather than a pretext to ignore asylum law. 

Migrant‑rights lawyers warn that the ruling effectively hands the president a shortcut around Congress: if rights switch on only after entry, then he can wall off the ports, keep people in Mexico, and claim the statutes simply don’t apply.

It’s not a one‑off. This is the second immigration case in one day that breaks in Trump’s favor, on top of earlier emergency rulings that let him deport people to third countries and revoke temporary legal status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans. 

Next up before the same Court: whether he can rewrite birthright citizenship. Case by case, the message is the same: rights for migrants are not things you have — they’re switches the executive can flip off with the right wording, while the Court nods along and calls it “ordinary meaning.”

So the new border rule is simple and cynically precise. If you make it over the line, you’re a problem for the asylum system. If you’re stuck one step short, you’re just another body on the wrong side of a legal sentence. The law says “arrive in the United States”; the Court says that’s a matter of centimeters, not of lives.
